title: Slotized activation streaming experiment log
content:
Summary:

This note captures an ad-hoc investigation into a new execution technique we prototyped: "slotized activation streaming". The goal was to evaluate whether slicing activations into streamable 'slots' and overlapping activation movement with expert routing can reduce end-to-end p95/p99 latency for long-context Llama/Mistral/Qwen workloads, particularly under MoE routing where fanout and prefetching interact poorly with KV cache and allocator pressure.

Motivation / problem statement:
- In long-context workloads (8k-64k tokens) we observe two recurring issues with MoE-enabled models: (1) large activation footprints causing GPU host<->device transfer stalls during decoding bursts, (2) routing-driven fanout that increases serialization overhead when waiting on remote expert readiness. Existing prefetching and KV caching reduce compute but don't fully hide the tail queueing that occurs when many requests trigger large fanouts simultaneously.

Concept (slotized activation streaming):
- Break per-token activations (FFN outputs, gated expert outputs) into small, ordered slots (e.g., 256–1024 element chunks) that can be immediately enqueued for DMA after a slot is produced by a kernel rather than waiting for the full activation tensor.
- Overlap the DMA of early slots with subsequent kernel computation for the rest of the token, and allow partial assembly on the receiving GPU/SM for earliest possible continuation.
- Combine with routing-aware scheduling: route table indicates expected expert fanout for the coming tokens; scheduler increases slot parallelism for high-fanout tokens to start moving slots earlier.

Hardware and software setup:
- Cluster: 4x A100 80GB per node, PCIe host; NVLink not used for cross-device in these runs (isolated nodes).
- Runtime: rbw-runtime/0.27.3-proto (feature branch: slotized-activation); CUDA 12.1; cuBLAS/cuDNN standard.
- Models: Llama-70B-Long (positional extension), Mistral-7B-Long (custom long-context variant), Qwen-14B-Long, and a small MoE prototype based on Mistral-MoE-Base (16 experts, top-2 gating).
- Workloads: synthetic long docs (mix of code and prose) with target sequence lengths [8k, 16k, 32k, 64k]; realistic sampling from customer chat logs (anonymized). Decoding: greedy and top-p=0.9 beamless generations to 2k additional tokens.
- Measurement harness: per-request traced events (kernel start/end, DMA submit/complete, routing decision time, prefetch hit/miss) aggregated into p50/p95/p99 latency histograms.

Baseline behavior (no slotization):
- Llama/Qwen single-model host: baseline p95 decode latency at seq=16k: 420ms per 1k tokens generated; p99 890ms. Throughput 78 tokens/s.
- Mistral-MoE (top-2): at seq=16k, p95 decode latency 680ms per 1k tokens; p99 1.8s. Throughput 45 tokens/s.
- Observed hot paths: KV cache misses causing PCIe page faults (rare but high cost), expert fanout serialization (per-expert enqueue waits), and large pinned buffer allocation stalls when activation allocations peak.

Slotization experiments and variants tested:
- S-A1 (naïve slotize): slot size 1024 floats, streaming enabled for FFN only.
- S-A2 (fine slot): slot size 256 floats, streaming for FFN + gated expert outputs.
- S-A3 (adaptive slot): slot size adapts to routing fanout (small slots for high-fanout tokens).
- S-A4 (prefetch-aware): S-A3 + route-informed early DMA credit reservation to NIC/p2p engine.

Key observations and metrics:
1) Latency tail reduction on MoE runs:
- S-A2 reduced Mistral-MoE p95 by ~28% at seq=16k (from 680ms -> 490ms per 1k generated), p99 reduced by ~42% (1.8s -> 1.05s).
- Throughput increased modestly from 45 -> 53 tokens/s.
- Rationale: smaller slots allowed earlier transfer of first portions of expert outputs, enabling downstream kernels on receiving devices to begin sooner and reduced queueing windows.

2) Impact on memory pressure and allocator stalls:
- S-A1 (large slots) improved average latency but caused more frequent GPU pinned allocation batches leading to occasional 100–300ms host stalls.
- S-A2 avoided that by keeping slot allocations within preallocated ring buffers, reducing allocation churn.

3) KV cache interaction:
- For Llama and Qwen (non-MoE) the benefit was smaller: S-A2 gave ~8–12% p95 reduction at 16k, and negligible p99 improvement. Explanation: these models are less fanout-bound; the dominant cost was attention kernel and KV cache lookup which are less amenable to slot streaming. However, for very long contexts (32k+), slotization reduced worst-case GC-like eviction stalls by allowing eviction-ordered streaming interleaving.

4) Routing scheduling synergy (S-A3 / S-A4):
- Combining slotization with route-informed scheduling produced the best results for mixed workloads: p95 reductions of 30–38% across model mixes, p99 down by ~45% on average.
- Notable improvement when multiple concurrent sessions caused overlapping high-fanout bursts: early-slot movement converted a previously serialized critical path into partial overlap.

5) CPU and PCIe bus utilization:
- Slotized runs showed increased PCIe transaction rate (~1.6x) but lower peak transfer sizes; bus congestion was not observed at our test scale, but we expect degradation if host CPU cannot sustain submit rates. CPU submit spin increased 6–12% depending on slot size.

Tradeoffs and limitations:
- Increased submit frequency: small slot sizes increase DMA submit throughput and CPU overhead. Fine slot sizes (<256 elements) begin to hurt end-to-end latency due to submit overhead.
- Complexity in correctness: partial assembly on the receiving side required careful ordering guarantees and reassembly barriers to avoid model state corruption in corner cases (we observed 2 intermittent off-by-one token artifacts in early prototyping).
- Not a silver bullet for attention-dominated non-MoE models at moderate sequence lengths (<8k).

Micro-profiling traces (selected):
- Example trace (Mistral-MoE, seq=32k): baseline shows wait_on_expert_ready latency spikes correlating with enqueue_waits of 120–240ms; after S-A2 these waits dropped to 10–30ms but DMA_wait increased from 2ms->18ms for many slots (acceptable).
- Kernel overlap windows increased by ~22% in good runs, giving downstream FFN kernels earlier inputs and reducing stall chains.

Correctness verification and regressions:
- Ran full model eval set (n=5k traces). Found two edge-case failure modes: (1) race when a preemption triggered a partial slot discard -> wrong token on subsequent generation; (2) route change mid-token causing slot reordering. Both addressed by adding sequence stamps and a small reclaim window and by enforcing route-stability checks in the scheduler.

Recommendations / actionable follow-ups:
1) Integrate adaptive slotization as an opt-in runtime flag for MoE models only, with conservative defaults (slot_size=256, prealloc_ring=true).
2) Add CPU-side batching of DMA submits for small-slot runs to amortize submit cost (coalesce submits every N slots or 200 microseconds).
3) Add a route-stability pre-check and a fallback path that disables slotization for tokens where routing was unstable across gating passes.
4) Expose telemetry (slot_submit_rate, slot_assembly_lag) to Console for customers or internal SRE to monitor slot-induced bus pressure.
5) Run cluster-scale soak tests with mixed workloads (up to 100 concurrent sessions on 8-node cluster) to validate no hidden bus or driver regressions.

Open questions / experiments to run next:
- How does slotization interact with quantized kernels (4-bit/8-bit) and fused FFN kernels that may produce outputs in different memory layouts? Hypothesis: layout transformations will reduce benefit unless we can stream in the target layout.
- Evaluate slotization over NVLink and multi-GPU p2p to see if larger clusters further amplify win or expose interconnect bottlenecks.
- Investigate adaptive slot sizing driven by live per-request telemetry (auto-tune slot size for minimal latency under load).

Notes on productionization risk and rollout plan:
- Risk: increased CPU submit load and driver's DMA behavior could reveal rare driver bugs. Mitigation: staged rollout with telemetry and quick kill-switch; canary on Dedicated clusters with low impact; default off for hosted API customers.
- Rollout phases: Canary (internal only, 2 weeks) -> Dedicated canary (customer opt-in) -> Gradual enable behind feature flag with auto-disable if slot_submit_rate exceeds threshold.

Appendix A: short reproducible checklist (for engineers)
- Checkout branch: runtime/slotized-activation-feature
- Build: make -j8 runtime_cuda; ensure CUDA 12.1
- Launch harness: experiments/slotized/run.sh --model mistral-moe --seq 16000 --variant S-A2 --workers 12 --trace-out traces/sa2_16000.json
- Collect: scripts/agg-trace.py traces/sa2_16000.json --metrics p50,p95,p99 --out sa2-summary.csv

Appendix B: quick numbers table (median of 3 runs)
- Mistral-MoE baseline (16k): p95 680ms, p99 1800ms, throughput 45 tok/s
- Mistral-MoE S-A2 (16k): p95 490ms, p99 1050ms, throughput 53 tok/s
- Llama-70B baseline (16k): p95 420ms, p99 890ms, throughput 78 tok/s
- Llama-70B S-A2 (16k): p95 370ms, p99 840ms, throughput 82 tok/s

If you want, I can extract the exact trace snippets (line-numbered) and a small visual diagram of slot flow for the PR description.

Author: Asha Patel (runtime perf)
